title: Trait tame residue and the closed-point Gysin generator
statement:
Let $\ell$ be a prime, $n\geq1$, $\Lambda=\mathbf Z/\ell^n\mathbf Z$, and let $V=\operatorname{Spec}R$ be an excellent strictly henselian discrete valuation trait with $\ell$ invertible [def-exc-excellent-ring, def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology, def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring]. Write $s,\eta$ for the closed and generic points and $i:s\hookrightarrow V$ for the inclusion. Use small etale derived categories and twists as in [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex]. Let $G$ be tame inertia, $A=\Lambda[[G]]$, $I=\ker(A\to\Lambda)$ and $\sigma$ a topological generator of $G$. For the constant sheaf, its supported cohomology is represented by
$$F(\Lambda)=[\Lambda\xrightarrow{1}\Lambda\xrightarrow{0}\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,\Lambda)]$$
in degrees $0,1,2$, and evaluation at $1-\sigma$ identifies the last term with $\Lambda$. Via $\Lambda(-1)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}}(G,\Lambda)$, the tame residue sends a character $\chi$ to the functional whose value at $1-\sigma$ is $\chi(\sigma)$. Under this model, the Gysin morphism of [lem-per-absolute-gysin-purity], $\operatorname{Cl}_i:\Lambda_s(-1)[-2]\to i^!\Lambda_V$ gives the same map to the degree-two term. In particular the normalized transition of [def-per-potential-dualizing-complex] satisfies
$$\operatorname{sp}_{\eta,s}(\Lambda_V)=\operatorname{Cl}_i(1)[2]:\Lambda\longrightarrow R\Gamma_s\Lambda_V(1)[2]$$
after geometric restriction and the identity identification $R\Gamma_\eta\Lambda_V=\Lambda$. This is an equality with the Gysin normalization, including its sign, independent of $\sigma$.

source.place: Expose XVII, sections 1.2.2–1.2.3 (the exact three-term model, evaluation at 1-sigma), Definition 1.2.3.1 and Proposition 2.4.2.1(a); Expose XVI, Definition 2.3.1 for the closed-point Gysin normalization.

proof.text: Choose a uniformizer $\pi$. The DVR definition gives a principal ideal domain which is not a field: it is Noetherian because every ideal is finitely generated. A nonzero prime ideal in a PID is maximal (factor a generator and use primality), and locality therefore leaves exactly $(0)$ and $(\pi)$. Thus $R$ has dimension one and maximal ideal generated by one element; its localization at $(0)$ is a field. The regular-local definition consequently makes $V$ regular, while $s$ is the spectrum of a field and is regular. The closed immersion $i$ is Cartier, cut out by the nonzerodivisor $\pi$, and has codimension one. These observations verify the regular affine hypotheses needed below; excellence and invertibility of $\ell$ are hypotheses of the item.

source.place: XVII 2.4.1–2.4.2, the regular trait and its closed point

proof.text: Apply the prime-power trait model to the constant sheaf. Both stalks are $\Lambda$, specialization is the identity, and wild and tame inertia act trivially. An augmentation-ideal element acts as zero, so the last differential is zero. This gives exactly $F(\Lambda)=[\Lambda\xrightarrow{1}\Lambda\xrightarrow{0}\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,\Lambda)]$ in degrees $0,1,2$. The cited freeness $A(1-\sigma)\simeq I$ makes evaluation at $1-\sigma$ an isomorphism to $\Lambda$. Projection onto degree two and inclusion from degree two are inverse up to the explicit contracting homotopy which is the identity from degree one to degree zero and zero elsewhere. In particular no extra cohomology or scalar occurs in passing to degree two.

For a character $\chi:G\to\Lambda$, define $q_\chi$ by $q_\chi(1-\sigma)=\chi(\sigma)$. In the normalized trait transition the wild averaging is the identity on the constant sheaf. The displayed definition of the transition therefore sends $\chi$ to $q_\chi$, exactly the evaluation formula in the statement. For the Tate line $L=\mu_{\ell^n}(\bar\eta)$ the same formulas apply: the signed Tate sheaf of the potential-complex definition is a rank-one locally constant line and is constant on this trait: the residue field is separably closed, $z^{\ell^n}-1$ has $\ell^n$ distinct residue roots, and henselian lifting gives all these roots as sections of $V$. They give the same basis on both stalks. Thus $L$ has trivial wild and tame action. The tensor/evaluation identification converts $\Lambda(-1)\to F(\Lambda)[2]$ into the specified $\Lambda\to F(\Lambda)(1)[2]$.

Keep track of the localization boundary. The finite-abelian $H^1$ classification identifies $H^1(\eta,L)$ with continuous characters of its absolute Galois group. For a tame character $c:G\to L$, the augmentation-cocycle comparison represents this degree-one class by $f_c\in\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,L)$ with $f_c(1-\sigma)=-c(\sigma)$, hence $f_c=-q_c$. Global sections on the strictly henselian $V$ have no positive cohomology. The localization triangle, together with the supported model of step 2, then gives no generic cohomology above degree one. Its degree-zero and degree-one modules are the two free rank-one modules $L$ and $\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,L)$. These give the two-term generic model $C=[L\xrightarrow{0}\operatorname{Hom}_A(I,L)]$ with the degree-one identification just specified: the ordinary truncation triangle splits since the degree-one module is projective (resolve it by itself in degree zero). In the signed fibre over $L[0]\to C$, the differentials before specializing to trivial action are $+1$ and minus the augmentation differential. The three-term trait model has $+1$ and plus that differential; their comparison is the identity in degrees zero and one and minus the identity in degree two. The signed-relative boundary $b\mapsto(0,-b)$ therefore becomes $+b$ in the trait model. In particular $\partial[c]$ is represented there by $f_c=-q_c$. The augmentation resolution fixes this comparison before the differentials vanish, so no arbitrary sign of a splitting is being chosen.

source.place: XVII 1.2.2–1.2.3, augmentation-model/localization comparison; explicit signed-fibre calculation

proof.text: On $\eta$ consider the torsor $z^{\ell^n}=\pi$. Its Kummer class is $\kappa(\pi)$; on a chosen geometric root $r$ its cocycle is $h\mapsto h(r)/r$. The tame quotient in the prime-power model is defined by the action on compatible prime-to-residue-characteristic roots of a uniformizer. Hence this cocycle factors through $G$ and equals its projection $c_\pi:G\to\mu_{\ell^n}=L$. For a topological generator $\sigma$, $c_\pi(\sigma)$ generates $L$. In the basis $c_\pi(\sigma)$, the character corresponding to the dual basis of $\Lambda(-1)$ has value $1$ at $\sigma$. Thus $q_{c_\pi}$ is exactly the image of $1\in\Lambda$ under the transition after the twist/evaluation identifications of step 3. This specifies the temporary Tate-line basis, without choosing a permanent trivialization.

source.place: XVI 2.1–2.3 and XVII 1.2.3; Kummer torsor of a uniformizer

proof.text: Apply the Cartier Gysin–Kummer comparison to $X=V$, $D=s$, and $f=\pi$; step 1 checked every regularity and Cartier hypothesis. It identifies the class of $\operatorname{Cl}_i(1)[2]$ with $-\partial\kappa(\pi)$ in the explicitly fixed signed-relative realization, using the Yoneda Chern convention stated in that comparison (the source permits a coherent choice of this convention). Step 4 computes $\partial\kappa(\pi)=-q_{c_\pi}$. Therefore the class of $\operatorname{Cl}_i(1)[2]$ is $q_{c_\pi}$, precisely the transition of step 5. This is an equality of derived morphisms: the supported-Hom identification realizes both classes as maps, and after the contraction of step 2 their common target is the degree-zero rank-one module $L\otimes\Lambda(-1)$. A map from the free rank-one source $\Lambda[0]$ is determined by the image of $1$ (its projective resolution is $\Lambda[0]$ itself). The two maps agree, including scalar and sign.

source.place: XVII Proposition 2.4.2.1(a), filling its sign comparison using XVI 2.3.1

proof.text: For the normalized transition on this trait, the reduced closure of the generic point is $V$ itself and its normalization is the identity: a DVR is integrally closed by its valuation description in the DVR definition (a negative-valuation integral element contradicts its monic equation, in which its highest power has strictly smallest valuation). The closed residue degree is $1$. The definition of the normalized transition supplies no extra factor. Geometric restriction at the generic point gives the constant stalk $\Lambda$, so the equality proved reads $\operatorname{sp}_{\eta,s}(\Lambda_V)=\operatorname{Cl}_i(1)[2]$ with the stated source and target. Independence of $\sigma$ follows from the generator-independent trait transition in the prime-power model; the Gysin class is intrinsic. No generator or uniformizer remains in this derived equality.

proof_origin.place: XVII 1.2.1–1.2.3 and Proposition 2.4.2.1(a); explicit signed comparison filling the abbreviated proof, via XVI 2.1–2.3

In the Gabber volume (ILO) I read XVI Def 1.1 with its sign footnote, Def 2.1.1, Defs 2.2.2.5/2.2.2.7 and Def 2.3.1, and XVII 1.2.1–1.2.3.2, 2.4.1.1 and 2.4.2.1(a); no SGA source is cited. The item statement is unchanged. Adding lem-per-prime-power-trait-residue-model to stmt_deps is justified: G, A, I and F are that node's objects, and def-per-potential-dualizing-complex already cites it. I recomputed the signs. (1) The cone fibre with D(a,b)=(da,res a-db) over L_s -> [L^S -> Hom_A(I,L^S)] maps to the three-term model F by the identity in degrees 0 and 1 and by -1 in degree 2. Composed with the inclusion of supported sections, this is ILO XVII 1.2.2.1's 'morphisme evident', so the boundary b->(0,-b) becomes +b in F. (2) The augmentation comparison f_c(g-1)=c(g) is the canonical bar-to-augmentation resolution map, so f_c(1-sigma)=-c(sigma). I proved the new augmentation node myself: choose an open normal U with c(U)=0, use the identity gh-1=(g-1)+g(h-1), and use density; edge cases are trivial G, finite cyclic G where I is not free, and trivial action with odd Lambda. (3) The Kummer cocycle of z^m=pi is h(r)/r, which matches lem-sc-torsor-h1's delta_T(1) convention and cor-galois-abelian-h1; it gives sp(1)=q_{c_pi}. (4) ILO XVI 2.2.2.5 with r=1 gives Cl_i=-c1(I,1)=+c1(O(D),s_D). In the Yoneda convention of def-asd-ordinary-supported-kummer-boundary, the corrected lem-pur-divisor-class computes this class locally as -boundary(kappa(f)), and the local boundary is the same as the cone b->(0,-b). So the new Cartier node's Cl_i(1)[2] = -boundary(kappa(f)) is the DAG's settled convention, and it agrees with the F_ell node lem-per-immersion-class-calculus (Cl = c_D). Its edge cases hold: a unit equation gives 0, and replacing f by uf leaves the class unchanged. Together these give sp = Cl, including the sign. Step 3's lifting of the m roots of unity follows from idempotent lifting in R[z]/(z^m-1); step 7 has d=1 because a DVR is normal. Duplicates: lem-per-prime-power-regular-gysin and lem-per-prime-power-closed-immersion-gysin have no signed comparison, and lem-exc-procyclic-two-term, lem-per-trait-tame-algebra and cor-galois-abelian-h1 state different facts. Neither new node restates a clause of the item. B1-B4, B9 (blueprint references) and the recorded searches are fine.
